20 Official James Bond Cars Ranked From Most Famous To Most Obscure

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2263 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Jalopnik

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Amazon MGM Studios is in charge of the latest tack the longstanding James Bond franchise will take, after paying $1 billion to the Broccoli family for creative control last year.
  • Industry observers note that and surely there will be a latest car for Bond to drive around looking cool.
  • While we don't yet know what car Pattinson, Robert Pattinson will be driving as 007, we can spend the next couple of years or more dreaming up what might make for a good Bond car in 2029 or 2030.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Amazon MGM Studios is in charge of the latest tack the longstanding James Bond franchise will take, after paying $1 billion to the Broccoli family for creative control last year. And that comes after spending $8.5 billion in 2022 on the MGM Studios merger, which garnered the Bezos firm control of Bond's back catalog and intellectual property. Amazon has tasked Oscar-nominated director Denis Villeneuve with helming the next Bond film, and this week signed actor Robert Pattinson as the new face of the franchise.

Industry observers note that and surely there will be a latest car for Bond to drive around looking cool. Maybe, if we're lucky, he'll have an extensive desert chase sequence through the Sahara or something, and he can take a Q-modified version of Aston Martin's new Dakar race car for a spin.

While we don't yet know what car Pattinson, Robert Pattinson will be driving as 007, we can spend the next couple of years or more dreaming up what might make for a good Bond car in 2029 or 2030. He famously drove a trio of Volvos in the Twilight series, running a C30, an XC60, and an S60 R-design. What else has Pattinson driven on-screen? Oh, nothing special, just the frickin' Batmobile!

Recent findings suggest that while we don't know what the future Bond will drive, we can take a look at Bond cars of the past and judge them on their merits. Some are much better than others, of course. I'm going to put them in order of most to least famous, and we can argue about it in the comments. Let me know what you think and tell me why I'm wrong.

Amidst the 1977 baddies-chasing-Bond action scene in the Roger Moore era's "The Spy Who Loved Me," James Bond adeptly dispatches a motorcycle, a car full of baddies (including Richard Kiel's Jaws), and a helicopter in the Italian countryside. Bond's heavily modified Lotus Esprit takes the chase underwater, surprising his passenger-seat companion, KGB agent Maj. Anya Amasova (Triple X, aka Barbara Bach).

According to recent reports, the Lotus had just launched to the public a year earlier, bringing hard-edged "folded paper" Giorgetto Giugiaro design and a 160-horsepower Type 907 2-liter four-cylinder engine to the street. The 2,200-pound Lotus was praised in its day for great handling and steering, the motoring press considered it underpowered. As far as I'm aware, however, Lotus did not build any submersible Esprits — that was all the doing of MI6's Q Branch.

Once at sea, the Lotus tucked away its wheels and sprouted fins and a periscope. With the press of a button, Bond debuted a torpedo straight upward at the hovering helicopter, blowing it to bits. This chase sequence seems a bit staid and underwhelming in 2026, but back in the late 1970s, it was positively the state of the art of action sequencing.

While many might argue that Bond is synonymous with a silver Aston Martin, the character has had so many different ones over the years that they all kind of blend together. He's driven lots of non-Astons, too! The submersible Lotus is, if you ask me, the one that is most easily identifiable as a specific Bond car, making it my choice for the most famous individual example. Feel free to let me know why you think I'm wrong.

According to recent reports, the iconic Aston Martin DB5 has been a pretty consistent piece of James Bond lore for decades. Co-starring more often than any other car, the DB5 has appeared in eight franchise films. Across the recent Daniel Craig series of Bond films, the DB5 made recurring guest spots in Bond's garage in "Casino Royale," "Skyfall," "Spectre," and "No Time To Die." It also co-starred with Pierce Brosnan in "GoldenEye" and "Tomorrow Never Dies." The car is perhaps most famous for its screen time in 1964's "Goldfinger" and 1965's "Thunderball," alongside Sean Connery's Bond.

"Goldfinger" set the standard for Bond cars, as it was the first time gadgets had been fitted. This car had an ejector seat, machine guns hidden behind the front turn-signal lamps, a rotating license plate display, rear-deployed smoke screen and oil slick, a bulletproof rear window screen, wheel blades for slashing tires, and an onboard homing system.

Industry observers note that when most people think about James Bond, they think of shaken dry martinis, Omega watches, a Walther PPK compact semi-automatic pistol, and a silver Aston Martin. The Aston is iconic, but perhaps because it is so subdued in its appearance, and because all of the individual Astons blend together in the zeitgeist, it isn't quite as famous as the Lotus.

An argument could certainly be made for the DB5 as the best-known Bond car, but the DB5 never went underwater, did it? In this case, I think the Lotus wins just for the cool factor, but it's a narrow victory. And perhaps a pyrrhic one, as Bond never again helmed a Lotus for a film. Aston has been with Bond for decades, and I'd be surprised if Pattinbond drives anything from another manufacturer.

It has been revealed that bond has also driven a DBS in "On Her Majesty's Secret Service,"  a V8 Vantage in 1987's "The Living Daylights," a V12 Vanquish in "Die Another Day," a modern DBS in "Casino Royale," a DB10 in "Spectre," and while he didn't drive it, Bond even had a Valhalla in "No Time To Die." About half of the films released have featured an Aston. It's hard to separate the character from the British manufacturer, by design. Aston has spent millions associating its products with the world's greatest spy.

In a recent development, perhaps the most famous use of an Aston in recent Bond films was the chase scene in "Casino Royale" (above) which sees Bond driving, and then crashing, the then-latest DBS revival. While running down baddies on a wet night road, Bond comes upon Eva Green's Vesper Lynd having been dumped in the middle of the road. To avoid her, Double-Oh-Seven manages to roll his car a then-Guinness-record seven times on-screen.

Aston hasn't been there for every Bond installment, and the relationship went dormant for some time. Since the Craig era of Bond began, Aston has been pumping up its connection with the franchise, promoting the tie-ins nearly as hard as it does now with its Formula 1 relationship. Because both parties seem to benefit from working together, it would take quite a lot of pull to separate them for future installments, I believe.

Sources indicate that of course, since the franchise is now under fresh ownership, things might change. Maybe Amazon will want Bond to drive a Slate truck or Rivian instead. Pattinson, meanwhile, has a personal relationship with watchmaker Jaeger-LeCoultre, so perhaps his Bond also won't be wearing the iconic Omega. At this point, the future of what Bond is could be decided by Jeff Bezos himself.

For a brief moment during the Brosnan era, Britain's licensed-to-kill spook drove German cars. When Brosnan got the role, he was cast in "GoldenEye" alongside BMW's small Z3 sports car decked out with plenty of weapons. Unfortunately, it was little more than paid product placement and was off-screen as promptly as it came, seemingly just there for the minimum required contractual time.

My favorite of the BondMWs was the long-wheelbase V12 7-series in "Tomorrow Never Dies." In an effort to thwart the baddies while maintaining his safety and security, Bond uses the car's fictional remote-control capabilities (with an Ericsson mobile phone trackpad!) to drive around from the rear seat. For years I wished I could do something similar with my own cars, despite it serving no purpose in my life. I'm not a spy, and I don't need to escape baddies (as far as you know), but it's cool nonetheless. This giant stately sedan met its end when Bond eventually drove it off a parking garage roof. I still want an E38-generation 7-series, just thinking about it now.

In a recent development, I'm going to get some guff for this, but Brosnan's BMW Z8 in "The World Is Not Enough" is, was, and always will be the best-looking car Bond ever drove on-screen. Like the Z3, this incredible grand tourer didn't really get enough screen time. What little time it did have, however, it looked stunning, and met an incredibly satisfying end. After using a fender-mounted rocket launcher to take down a helicopter, a second helicopter fitted with tree-trimming saws sliced the Bimmer in half (pictured above)!

It's unlikely we'll ever see Bond in a BMW again, and that's probably a good thing. Could you imagine him driving a newly introduced X6 M Competition? I shudder at the thought.

It has been revealed that the collective Jaguar and Land Rover brands have been important to the Bond franchise over the last few decades, having provided quite a few vehicles for bad guys and henchmen to make chase in across several films. As far as I can tell, Bond only ever drove one Jaguar, the State-provided long-wheelbase XJ that Craig uses to "kidnap" M and abscond to the Skyfall estate in an effort to stay one step ahead of Raoul Silva. The car is on-screen for just over a minute before the pair swap to Bond's personal Aston Martin DB5. There's a reason the Jag is so far down the list, of course, as he barely drives it, and there's very little action happening.

Despite Aston and Lotus handily smashing Jaguar on the cool factor when it comes to Bond cars, Jag's involvement as the car of choice for international baddies definitely ups the leaping cat's cool quotient a bit. Think back to "Die Another Day" and you'll have seen henchman Tang Lin Zao driving a bright green Jaguar XKR fitted with Bond-level gadgets, including grille rocket launchers, a minigun, and thermal imaging. It wasn't a match for Bond's invisible Aston Vanquish on ice, but it was still very cool to see.

According to recent reports, do you remember when wrestler-turned-actor Dave Bautista became a Bond villain in "Spectre"? Along with his brawn, Bautista also brought an eye-catching hypercar to the franchise with the Jaguar CX75 concept taking the fight to Bond's malfunctioning never-sold-to-the-public Aston DB10.

In a recent development, both cars are absolutely spectacular to look at, but the chase is a little underwhelming. Bond eventually has to sink the Aston and use the ejector seat button to escape Bautista's character Hinx.

Recent findings suggest that you'd be forgiven for never really associating Bond with American cars, but he's definitely driven them a few times. Most of these scenes were filmed before I was born, in an era when Bond movies were much more camp than the nonstop action set pieces they are today. While the Bond books were always pretty interesting, the movies tended toward the absurd, particularly in the early days.

In what is perhaps the most nonsensical move in all of James Bond history, Roger Moore's "The Man with the Golden Gun" came with American Motors Corporation product placement and a "Dukes Of Hazzard"-style bridge jumping sequence. Bond steals a 1974 AMC Hornet X from a dealership in an effort to chase down the bad guy's AMC Matador. When he needs to cross a river and the bridge is out, Bond lines up and puts pedal to the metal, going for style points in the process. If you ask me, this scene could have done without the slide-whistle sound effect. The stunt was pretty stunning, however, as stunt performer extraordinaire Loren Willert managed the jump in one take (above).

In a recent development, I've lived in snowy winter climates all my life, and I'm not sure I've heard squealing tires quite like what happens in the Switzerland ice-racing sequence from "On Her Majesty's Secret Service." In spite of the bad use of Foley art in the sequence (and the poor Ford Escort that ends up on its roof), it remains one of my favorite old-school moments in a Bond film. Even better, it wasn't Bond driving at the time.

Call me crazy, but I think the cars Bond drives in the original Ian Fleming novels are significantly cooler than whatever Aston Martin he's driving this week. These are, sadly, the least famous of them all, because literacy is falling and regular reading is at its lowest level in decades. Please, go pick up a book, folks!

In the early books, namely "Casino Royale," "Live and Let Die," and "Moonraker," James Bond drives a 1930 4.5-liter Blower Bentley. While Bond's Bentley is mechanically identical to those driven by the Bentley Boys to Le Mans victory in the 1920s, his was painted battleship grey, while the racers were traditional British Racing Green. After a brief affair with a Bentley Mark IV Drophead Coupe, Bond settles on a supercharged Bentley Mark II Continental he calls "The Locomotive" that he maintains through the rest of the original 14-novel run.

Sources indicate that once John Gardner took over writing Bond novels in 1981, the character acquired the "Silver Beast," a Saab 900 Turbo, which he kept for much of the official book series run. Jalopnik has described the car as "the most obscure James Bond car of all time" and I can't help but agree with that sentiment 14 years later. With over 240 horsepower and a top speed of 170 miles per hour, it's a pretty rad little machine. Maybe, if we beg, Jeff Bezos will let the next Bond car be a highly modified 1980s Saab 900 Turbo.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 11:45 EST / NOVEMBER 19 2026.

According to recent reports, chinese biotech robotics firm MegaRobo Co. Ltd. today unveiled it has raised $200 million in fresh funding to invest in its core technology and expand its automated life sciences infrastructure for increasingly complex physical systems.

Founded in 2016, MegaRobo builds robotic systems that let artificial intelligence software run physical experiments, alongside precision measurement and inspection tools for manufacturers.

It has been revealed that investors joining the round included Oman Investment Authority, Asia Investment Capital, Granite Asia, Sinovation Ventures and CMB International. The tech giant raised $600 million to date across multiple funding rounds, including nearly $300 million in Series C during 2022.

“The first generation of AI learned from humanity’s accumulated knowledge. The next generation will increasingly learn by acting in the physical world — through experiments, production and continuous feedback,” said founder and Chief Executive Daniel Huang. “That shift changes AI from a system that interprets the world into one that can help create new knowledge, materials, processes and products.”.

In a recent development, the tech giant’s two most prominently marketed offerings are Megalaxy Lab, an AI-connected experimental platform and CellVue T2000, its automated cell-imaging instrument. Both appear on the company’s English-language homepage. MegaRobo also sells more specialized lab equipment, including the Auflo sample-preparation workstation and the Seloris cell culturing automation system.

The key distinction is that Megalaxy Lab is the public face for the manufacturer’s AI-for-science strategy, while CellVue and other systems represent concrete examples of the instruments it builds for the industry.

The company said through Megalaxy it is making real-world experimentation programmable and accessible. Researchers and AI agents can configure experiments, route them through automated laboratory systems, track execution, receive structured, machine-readable results, and feed them directly into the next cycle of scientific reasoning. This includes virtual large data readouts that can be amplified as digital twins representing the scientific data, protein design, biochemistry and other properties.

Sources indicate that megaRobo said it’s working together with industry partners, including Tencent Cloud and Twist Bioscience, to expand its capability in the AI Science community with the launch of Poreva Open, a global AI protein design challenge open to all models and technical approaches. Megalaxy will provide wet-lab validation for more than 10,000 protein design sequences, creating an opportunity to test models against real experimental data.

Industry observers note that the company is also developing the One Intelligence Stack as a common technology foundation for instruments, machines, materials processes and real-world feedback. It’s not just a collection of isolated AI applications and products, but a chain infrastructure that enables AI to act, learn and observe across complex physical environments.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Sources indicate that “Project Olmedo will give AGCO long-term price certainty for the majority of the electricity certificate cost in Europe,” said Tim Millwood, Senior Vice President, Chief Supply Chain Officer.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

OLMEDO, Spain, Nov. 19, 2026 — AGCO (NYSE: AGCO) today announced that Project Olmedo, the solar installation at the center of its first Virtual Power Purchase Agreement (VPPA), has completed construction and commissioning and is expected to begin delivering renewable electricity to the Spanish power grid in the coming months, pending final regulatory approvals. BRUC, one of the largest renewable energy groups in Spain, built the new solar installation in the northwest province of Valladolid.

Industry observers note that the milestone follows AGCO’s September 2025 announcement of its 10-year VPPA with BRUC. The installation’s two solar projects, Los Silos and El Granero, span approximately 300 hectares (741 acres) and hold approximately 150,000 solar panels. AGCO’s portion of the installation’s annual production is expected to be approximately 150 gigawatt-hours (GWh) of renewable electricity a year, equivalent to the annual electricity consumption of approximately 40,000 European households, based on Eurostat data.

Sources indicate that “Project Olmedo will give AGCO long-term price certainty for the majority of the electricity certificate cost in Europe,” said Tim Millwood, Senior Vice President, Chief Supply Chain Officer. “In volatile energy markets, securing that stability for 10 years strengthens the resilience of our supply chain while supporting latest renewable generation.”.

A VPPA lets a company support new renewable energy projects without taking direct delivery of the electricity they generate. Because AGCO’s agreement supported the construction of a brand-new installation, it will add new renewable capacity to the grid rather than drawing on existing sources, a principle known as additionality. The agreement also helps reduce AGCO’s Scope 2 greenhouse gas emissions from purchased electricity in its Europe/Middle East (EME) region and supports its commitment to reduce absolute Scope 1 and 2 emissions by 55% by 2033 from a 2022 baseline.

It has been revealed that “Additionality is what makes this agreement truly meaningful,” mentioned Roger Batkin, Senior Vice President, Corporate Affairs, General Counsel & Corporate Secretary. “We did not simply buy renewable electricity that already existed; we supported the construction of a brand-latest renewable solar project. Accomplishing this project required over two years of involvement from many teams, functions, and areas of expertise across AGCO, along with technical advisory support from Schneider Electric and a strong partnership with BRUC.”.

Reflecting AGCO’s Farmer-First strategy, Project Olmedo supports local farmers to further diversify their land use by leasing land for the project while maintaining the option for livestock to graze among the panels, maintaining the vegetation in place of machinery.

AGCO and BRUC leaders, joined by local community representatives José Emilio Escudero García, Mayor of Bocigas, and Ursino Vara Pérez, Mayor of Almenara de Adaja, marked the milestone with a ribbon-cutting ceremony at the site in November. Additional drone footage from Project Olmedo and the ribbon-cutting event are available on AGCO’s YouTube page.

Industry observers note that for more details on AGCO’s sustainability initiatives, visit the company’s sustainability webpage and read the 2025 Sustainability Report. For more information about BRUC, visit the company’s website at brucenergy.com.

AGCO (NYSE: AGCO) is a global leader in agricultural machinery and precision agriculture technologies. Driven by a Farmer-First strategy, AGCO delivers value through its differentiated leading brands, Fendt™, Massey Ferguson™, PTx™ and Valtra™. AGCO’s high-performance equipment and smart farming solutions, including brand-agnostic retrofit technologies and autonomous offerings, empower farmers to drive productivity while sustainably feeding the world. For more information, visit www.agcocorp.com.

According to recent reports, the U.S. Dept. of the Interior has immediately paused the leases for all large-scale offshore wind projects under construction in the United States due to “national security risks identified by the Dept. of War in recently completed classified reports.”.

In a recent development, “The prime duty of the United States government is to protect the American people,” stated Secretary of the Interior Doug Burgum. “Today’s action addresses emerging national security risks, including the rapid evolution of the relevant adversary technologies, and the vulnerabilities created by large-scale offshore wind projects with proximity near our East Coast population centers. The Trump administration will always prioritize the security of the American people.”.

The following leases are paused:.

The Dept. of the Interior claims that the blade movement and reflective towers create “radar interference called ‘clutter.'” Allegedly, this is a national security risk.

Dominion Energy released the following statement in response to the pause issued for the Coastal Virginia Offshore Wind project:.

According to recent reports, “The Coastal Virginia Offshore Wind Project (CVOW) is essential for American national security and meeting Virginia’s dramatically growing energy needs, the fastest growth in America. This growth is driven by the need to provide reliable power to many of America’s most key war fighting installations, the world’s largest warship manufacturer, and the largest concentration of data centers on the planet as well as the leading edge of the AI revolution.

Sources indicate that stopping CVOW for any length of time will threaten grid reliability for some of the nation’s most important war fighting, AI and civilian assets. It will also lead to energy inflation and threaten thousands of jobs.

CVOW is American-owned and benefits all of our Virginia customers. Our customers are paying for the project after a careful review of project costs and benefits by Virginia state regulators in 2022. These same state regulators, along with numerous federal agencies, oversee our cyber and physical security program, which is among the strongest in the energy industry.

Industry observers note that the project has been more than 10 years in the works, involved close coordination with the military, and is located 27 to 44 miles offshore, so far offshore it does not raise visual impact concerns. The project’s two pilot turbines have been operating for five years without causing any impacts to national security.

CVOW enjoys bipartisan support and is within months of generating a massive 2,600 MW to support the fastest growing part of America’s energy grid. This growth serves the largest concentration of critical infrastructure in the world.

Virginia’s All-American, All-Of-The-Above-Energy Blueprint requires a range of power generation assets, including natural gas, advanced nuclear, and renewables. Virginia needs every electron we can get as our demand for electricity doubles. These electrons will power the data centers that will win the AI race, support our war fighters, and build the nuclear warships needed to maintain our maritime supremacy. Virginia’s grid needs addition of electrons, not subtraction.

We stand ready to do what is necessary to get these vital electrons flowing as quickly as possible.”.

In response, Sierra Club Executive Director Loren Blackford released the following statement:.

#88355. Here's How The White Boxes On Traffic Lights Help Traffic Flow

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (778 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Jalopnik ↗ Open Full Page

Here's How The White Boxes On Traffic Lights Help Traffic Flow

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (778 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Jalopnik

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that you are being tracked.
  • Sources indicate that the good news is these white boxes are radar-based and relatively low-tech compared to the AI-powered automated license plate readers (ALPRs) that collect more data than necessary.
  • Industry observers note that also called stop bar sensors or stop boxes, these aboveground radar presence detectors (RPDs) are essentially weatherproof.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that you are being tracked. Even if you didn't agree to the Terms & Conditions, Big Brother is surveilling you anyway. And it doesn't need cameras or a microphone to do so. Case in point: white rectangular panels perched alongside traffic lights. Although the information they gather is used less nefariously than data from the more than 100,000 Flock cameras that dot U.S. roadways, they still monitor your vehicle's movements.

Sources indicate that the good news is these white boxes are radar-based and relatively low-tech compared to the AI-powered automated license plate readers (ALPRs) that collect more data than necessary. The less intrusive white radar units strictly monitor traffic flow, which is why they're found near or at intersections. Flock devices, on the other hand, are so widespread that DeFlock, an open-source mapping project, was created to educate the public on their locations.

Industry observers note that also called stop bar sensors or stop boxes, these aboveground radar presence detectors (RPDs) are essentially weatherproof. Standard traffic control cameras, on the other hand, can be compromised during foggy or rainy days. These easy-to-maintain RPDs are used in conjunction with other traffic light sensors and congestion-monitoring technology. All of these gizmos and gadgets are making traffic light mounts resemble bird-heavy power lines, but can also be intimidating to an already leery public concerned about privacy concerns. Thankfully, RPDs don't care about where you're going or coming from, only that, well, you leave.

Many of these white-box sensors are developed by Wavetronix, a Utah-based manufacturer specializing in radar traffic detection and monitoring systems. Part of its Intersection Performance System lineup are two types of panel-style monitors.

According to recent reports, featuring a large flat panel, the SmartSensor Matrix utilizes 16 beams and supports just as many zones and channels. With a 140-foot range and a 90-degree field of view, the Matrix can track up to 10 lanes individually and takes about 10 minutes to install. The SmartSensor Advance offers a more focused single radar that tracks up to three lanes, but with a 600-foot standard range that extends to 900 feet with the Advance Extended Range model for large vehicles like buses and trucks. The Advance can also prolong a green light to allow lagging cars to pass the intersection safely as well as keep traffic from blocking access to fire stations and hospitals.

Recent findings suggest that weighing 4.2 and 3.8 pounds, respectively, both the Matrix and the Advance are 13 inches long, 10.6 inches wide, and 3 to 4 inches thick. Plus, they're basically set-it-and-forget-it products. They need no cleaning, battery replacement, or recalibration, and the mean time between failures is an estimated 10 years.

However, Wavetronix radars do cost more upfront than Flock cameras. In Dubuque, Iowa, after installation began in 2008, the city had more than 20 intersections equipped with Matrix sensors by 2015, with four devices used at a typical intersection. Wavetronix doesn't publish its pricing, but in a 2015 Telegraph Herald interview, the city traffic engineer noted the devices cost about $5,000 apiece. When Flock cameras get damaged, taxpayers are billed $800 per camera and between $500 and $2,000 for the pole. The radar return on investment, though, is that your commute remains your business.

If you're worried about what else these white boxes are monitoring, don't be. Like white hat hackers, RPDs are about improving our quality of life and not about helping your ex stalk you — the information is gathered solely for traffic mitigation purposes and specific to the intersection. They are used by traffic engineers, not by law enforcement. In 2022, Springfield, Missouri, had about 60 radar sensors in use at various intersections and planned to install 33 more.

Sources indicate that to quell public concern at the time, the city's traffic engineer, Tom Dancey, told local news station KYTV, "These are just radar units, that would be picking up the presence of the moving vehicle that's approaching the intersection. So the information is just tied to the traffic signal system, it's in no way being used for enforcement. The data that we're collecting from that is traffic or traffic counts.".

Wavetronix devices simply capture traffic data and nothing more. No images of your license plate or tracking of the route of your vehicle at every corner. So, there's no need to vandalize them like license plate readers or cover vehicle trackers with garbage bags, though Flock's infrared cameras can still record while under wraps. With these white boxes, you're just part of the headcount, a mere blip on a screen. Who knew being relegated to a basic statistic could feel so refreshing?

Beverly Hills Penthouse Sells for $21 Million in Enclave’s Most Expensive Condo Deal of the Year

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1031 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Realtor

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A Rosewood Residences branded penthouse has sold for $21 million, setting a record in the elite Los Angeles enclave of Beverly Hills.
  • After only 10 days on the market, Penthouse C at Rosewood Residences Beverly Hills has officially sold for $21 million, discounted from $27.5 million, making it the most expensive developer-sold condominium deal in Beverly Hills this year.
  • In a recent development, at $4,469 per square foot, the transaction ranks as the fifth-highest condominium sale in Los Angeles history by price per square foot.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A Rosewood Residences branded penthouse has sold for $21 million, setting a record in the elite Los Angeles enclave of Beverly Hills.

After only 10 days on the market, Penthouse C at Rosewood Residences Beverly Hills has officially sold for $21 million, discounted from $27.5 million, making it the most expensive developer-sold condominium deal in Beverly Hills this year.

In a recent development, at $4,469 per square foot, the transaction ranks as the fifth-highest condominium sale in Los Angeles history by price per square foot. Only 18 condominiums have ever sold for more than $20 million in the city.

"It was a very quick purchase," sales co-agent Amir Ensani of The Fridman Group at The Beverly Hills Estates tells Realtor.com®. The median days on market is 57, according to Realtor.com data.

Ensani claims the buyer, a man in the hospitality industry and his family, was—like all of the buyers in the boutique building—downsizing from a local "megaestate.".

"The big thing that caught the buyer was a staff of 22 with armed guards," notes the luxury broker. Additionally, the buyer, like many other high-net-worth individuals, was migrating to Beverly Hills in part because it has no so-called "mansion tax.".

Enacted in April 2023, the measure imposes a 4% tax on property sales of $5.4 million to $10.9 million, and a 5.5% tax on sales exceeding $10.9 million. These rates apply on top of Los Angeles' standard 0.45% base real estate transfer tax.

The buyer was also a fan of Rosewood Hotels, a global luxury hospitality brand. In Upcoming York, the company is behind The Carlyle. It does not have a Los Angeles location.

"It's like a double brand," the agent says about living not only inside of the full service Rosewood Residences but the separately incorporated city of Beverly Hills.

"A lot of the clients are Rosewood connoisseurs, including this one," he says. "They are accustomed to a level of service that Rosewood provides.".

The Rosewood Residences is the only stand-alone residential complex for the brand in the world, a significant plus for the property, notes the broker.

"A lot of people who love the brand may not want a hotel component, with people coming and going," he claims.

Another selling point was that the building is a "pedigree property," built on the site of the former Beverly Hills Friars Club, with interiors designed by Upcoming York-based designer Samuel Amoia.

"He likes to collect pedigree properties," Ensani claims of the buyer. "When he saw it, he was like 'I must have it.'".

The three-bedroom, five-full bathroom penthouse blends sculptural furnishings, collectible art, natural materials, and seamless indoor-outdoor living.

It boasts nearly 4,700 square feet indoors and 2,200 square feet of outdoor space with 25-foot private pool and hot tub, as well as a custom skylit floating staircase, a double-sided fireplace in carved stone, and a private rooftop with a spa and an outdoor kitchen.

The penthouse comes with $18,740 in monthly dues (property taxes not included).

With just 17 residences, the boutique building offers plenty of privacy—the penthouse comes with a private four-car garage—as well as security (the aforementioned armed guards).

The amenity suite includes butler service, personalized fitness training, in-residence spa treatments, house car and driver, valet service, and private chefs.

Next year, the building will welcome two Japanese dining concepts, including a steakhouse and an izakaya (Japanese bar and casual dining).

Colisting agent Tomer Fridman claims the units were designed as "estate alternatives" for affluent buyers accustomed to 30,000-square-foot mansions. (Sally Forster Jones of Forster Jones International & Associates at Compass also headed up sales at the complex.).

"These aren't pieds-à-terre with small galley kitchens," he indicates. "They were designed specifically for an audience that is accustomed to huge estates.".

In a recent development, the smallest unit is around 3,200 square feet with around 300 feet of outdoor space, and they top out at 7,200 square feet with 2,400 square feet of outdoor space. Fridman notes it is only one of two condo buildings in Los Angeles with these types of "estate alternative" offerings.

The broker says the generous proportions helped account for the complex's brisk sales, which closed on more more than 50% in presales, a milestone the agency says is unmatched by another LA condominium condo building in the past decade. (The sales team wouldn't say the current percentage of closed sales.).

Sources indicate that the estate-like units mean that downsizers can often bring much of their furniture with them—though Penthouse C came fully furnished and curated by the designer himself. Amoia previously designed the architect Robert A.M. Stern building at 520 Park Ave.

Despite the buyers downshifting from sprawling estates, Ensani says there is no singular demographic in the building. "We have families, we have people who are 20, we have people who are 80," he says.

While both agents agree that Los Angeles typically isn't a "condo market,"—with wealthy people historically preferring grand estates on large plots of land—it is becoming one.

Wildfires, the difficulty and expense of procuring insurance, and the expense and challenges of managing staff and maintenance, means that full service condos are becoming much more in demand.

According to recent reports, "You have to show buyers that they aren't giving up amenities," says Ensani. "They are used to sceening and entertainment rooms. You have to show them they are gaining services, and someone else will take care of them for you.".

Recent findings suggest that penthouse E, which is even larger than Penthouse C, spanning 5,817 interior square feet and 2,442 square feet of private outdoor space, will soon hit the market. The price hasn't been released.

Industry News: The EV Takeover Is Taking Shape, Despite Heroic Efforts To Stop It

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1118 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cleantechnica

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Whelp, the AI boom has had one positive knock-on effect.
  • According to recent reports, I’m just going to stick my neck out and say that the eponymous Aptera solar-powered autocycle from the US startup Aptera will attract enough AI-enriched drivers to make a go of it.
  • According to recent reports, autocycles were once common here in the US and overseas markets, distinguished from motorcycles by their front-facing seats and steering wheels, rather than straddled seats and handlebars.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Whelp, the AI boom has had one positive knock-on effect. It is creating fresh multi-millionaires by the bushel, any one of whom can afford to splurge on a pricey new electric vehicle. That aside, EV stakeholders in the US are springing back to life after a year-long slumber. Even General Motors is in play, stirring up long lost memories of its 1990’s-era EV1 debacle instead of hiding its head in shame. What’s up with that?

According to recent reports, I’m just going to stick my neck out and say that the eponymous Aptera solar-powered autocycle from the US startup Aptera will attract enough AI-enriched drivers to make a go of it. The on-again, off-again, on-again automaker has been on this year, working towards volume production of a plug-in, three-wheeled two-seater EV that can travel up to 40 miles on its own solar-plus-storage system (see more Aptera news here).

According to recent reports, autocycles were once common here in the US and overseas markets, distinguished from motorcycles by their front-facing seats and steering wheels, rather than straddled seats and handlebars. They fell out of favor in the US by the middle of the 20th century, but 21st century hot-rodders have revived the form with a focus on eyebrow-raising, open-air, gas-guzzling showpieces. In particular, interest has spread in states that do not require autocycle drivers to invest in an additional motorcycle license.

It has been revealed that the Aptera is showy in its own right, resembling a rocket ship with unique aerodynamic styling. Perhaps it may even show up in the next James Bond adventure with James Pattinson at the wheel. In the meantime, the firm has just made good on its pledge to reward early investors in the world’s first solar-powered car with the first production models to role off the assembly line. Aptera #1 goes to the founder and CEO of GDP Venture, Martin Hartono, aka “Accelerator #1.”.

According to recent reports, drivers can reserve an Aptera of their own for just $100, and they can expect to pay about $40,000 for the ride. Considering that the solar fuel is free, anyone in the mood for a head-turning ride will get quite a bargain for their $40,000 compared to other competitors in the zero emission two-seater field, such as the recently refreshed Tesla Roadster.

Speaking of refresh, General Motors has been weirdly lavishing attention on the EV1 sedan all this year, even though the automaker has been roundly criticized for the killing the short-lived car in its cradle. The automaker began producing EV1 electric sedans starting in 1996, following the unveiling of its Impact electric concept car in 1990. Unlike the Impact, EV1 was designed for use on the road. However, it was also designed mainly for the California market, and primarily for lease, not for sale. Production halted in 2003 at just about 1,000 vehicles, all to be recalled by GM and sent to the crusher as chronicled in Chris Paine’s 2006 documentary, “Who Killed The Electric Car?”.

In a recent development, or, maybe not so weird after all. GM’s electrification journey long predates the launch of Tesla Motors in 2003. The legacy automaker is now determined to stake out its claim on automotive history, with 2026 marking the 30th anniversary of the start of EV1 production.

GM has been celebrating the anniversary all this year with multiple long form articles about the Impact and EV1 on its website, eager to remind everybody that its industry-leading vehicle electrification efforts of the 1990’s continue to manifest decades later, in the form of heat pumps for climate control, by-wire technology, and regenerative braking among other elements.

Recent findings suggest that GM’s latest love letter to the EV1 popped up on November 17, when the automaker officially celebrated the completed restoration of the EV1 “V212” alongside its a private owner, Billy Caruso. The rare survivor of GM’s the junkyard crusher was evidently hiding out in an impound lot in Georgia all these years, until Caruso acquired it at auction and enlisted Jared Pink of the popular show The Questionable Garage to fix it up. Considering TQG’s large following on YouTube, GM wisely lent its engineers to the effort, along with several donated parts from its own EV1.

It has been revealed that US President Donald Trump and the Republican majority in Congress have made a heroic effort to dial down the vehicle electrification movement, but facts on the ground keep getting in their way. For starters, today’s advanced batteries apply across multiple energy resources, fossil and non-fossil alike. So, it’s no surprise to see the US Department of Energy continuing to throw taxpayer dollars at fresh energy storage projects (here’s one example), even though some of that activity will eventually ripple into the vehicle electrification field.

The US Department of Defense is also getting into the act. DoD’s electrification journey has been a tedious one, but in recent years it has begun creeping stealthily towards a vision of ground mobility enabled by electricity, providing the key tactical advantages of silent running and a low heat signature.

The latest news on that score involves a $1.4 billion loan commitment from DoD’s Office of Strategic Capital (OSC), enabling the silicon-based battery materials startup Sila to vault its signature product into commercial production. DoD’s primary interest in the tech giant consists of applications in the electric drone and autonomous mobility fields, but Sila has long been eyeballing the EV market as well.

It has been revealed that sila secured the loan commitment in August, and it has not let the grass grow under its feet. On November 18 the manufacturer announced an off-take agreement with the well-known Tesla EV battery supplier Panasonic Energy Corporation of North America. “The multi-year agreement is part of a long-term commercial relationship with the potential for over $1 billion of offtake over time,” Sila explained in a press statement, further elaborating that Panasonic will deploy its proprietary Titan Silicon silicon-carbon anode material in battery cells.

According to recent reports, “The partnership is also expected to support significant manufacturing and construction job creation in the United States. With Sila’s U.S.-based anode production underpinned by proprietary American technology and know-how, Panasonic and its OEM customers gain a clearer path toward a more secure, resilient, and sustainable domestic supply chain,” Sila emphasized.

That’s…interesting! Aside from Tesla as one of Sila’s OEM customers, keep an eye on another Panasonic offtaker, the up-and-comer US startup Harbinger Motors, which also has a foot in the DoD door.

Photo: The vehicle electrification movement is far from over in the US, with the startup Aptera among the stakeholders betting on an EV sales rebound in the coming years (cropped, courtesy of Aptera).

#88352. 7 6.2-Liter V8s Ranked From Least To Most Horsepower

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1598 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Jalopnik ↗ Open Full Page

7 6.2-Liter V8s Ranked From Least To Most Horsepower

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1598 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Jalopnik

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The 6.2-liter V8 holds a special place in the hearts of modern muscle-car fans.
  • It has been revealed that true, some V8-powered supercars can top the horsepower output from these 6.2-liter units.
  • It has been revealed that we do have a disclaimer, though.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The 6.2-liter V8 holds a special place in the hearts of modern muscle-car fans. After all, a motor that size was under the hood of the dearly departed third-generation Dodge Challenger — in which it showed off a horsepower rating well into four-figure territory — and Dodge isn't the only automaker to use a beefy 6.2-liter V8.

It has been revealed that true, some V8-powered supercars can top the horsepower output from these 6.2-liter units. The Hennessey Venom F5, for one, touts 1,817 horses from its 6.6-liter twin-turbo V8. But 6.2-liter V8s, whether they're naturally aspirated, turbocharged, or supercharged, are among some of the most powerful and most well-liked powerplants of all time. We'll get into the details below, but there are all sorts of rides like the Ford F-150 Raptor, the first mid-engine Chevrolet Corvette, the Chevy Camaro ZL-1, and various Mercedes-Benz AMG models ranging from the C 63 to the SLS AMG that use impressive 6.2-liter V8s.

It has been revealed that we do have a disclaimer, though. Engine displacement is generally displayed in cubic liters today, but many automakers do their measuring in terms of cubic centimeters. Then they round up to get to liters. For instance, Dodge's 6.2-liter Hemi V8 actually displaces closer to 6,166 cubic centimeters, so the numbers aren't hyper-precise, but we figure it's close enough.

The trail-ready Ford F-150 SVT Raptor hit dealerships in 2010 with an optional 6.2-liter unit capped at 400 hp. Ford then made that engine standard, with 411 ponies, the following year. Known by Blue Oval fans and insiders as "the Boss" – though it was unrelated to the V8s of the Boss Mustangs — it could propel the Raptor from zero to 60 mph in 6.6 seconds.

Recent findings suggest that ford started the engine's development with a goal of producing a so-called Triple Seven – a 7.0-liter V8 capable of 700 hp with a redline of 7,000 rpm. The single example made, many years later, would find its way into a 2005 Ford Mustang dragster that could get through the quarter mile in under 9 seconds. Who knows what kind of numbers the Raptor would have put up if Ford's 7.0-liter ended up under the hood? Even without it, though, the big-power pickup truck was an impressive rig.

Industry observers note that for a certain subset of AMG enthusiasts, this is where it all started. The naturally aspirated 6.2-liter M156 V8 was the first motor ever developed from scratch by MB's in-house performance division. All previous AMG vehicles had relied on modified Mercedes-Benz production engines. Of course, many of those engines were built by hand. The Mercedes-AMG philosophy of "one man, one engine" goes back to at least 1976, when the tech giant had relocated to Affalterbach, Germany.

Recent findings suggest that as for the first car with the M156, that distinction goes to the 2007 Mercedes-AMG E63, which won Car and Driver's German Sports Sedan Comparo that same year. No doubt impacting the decision, the naturally aspirated engine kicked out a healthy 507 hp and 446 pound-feet of torque. When C&D put that output to the test, the car released to 60 in a mere 4.2 seconds, dispatching the quarter mile in 12.6 seconds at 115 mph. By 2010, the E63's M156 came with 518 hp complemented by 465 lb-ft of torque.

In a recent development, the M156 would end up motivating the likes of the R230 SL 63 AMG, the CLK 63, CL 63, CLS 63, and ML 63, but it's important to note that the "63" attached to these machines was a bit of a misnomer. The M156's displacement remained at 6.2 liters in all these applications.

Industry observers note that the M159 started out with healthy horsepower, and it increased in output over the years. When the car premiered in 2010, its engine could make 563 horsepower, and the AMG SLS GT could serve up 583 horses from 2013-2015.

The 6.2-liter V8 powering the 2020 Mercedes-AMG SLS Black Series made 622 horsepower, which might seem meager by modern supercar standards, but that power output comes from a naturally aspirated mill. What's more, this engine wasn't simply an updated version of the M156 6.2-liter V8. The significant updates ranged from dry-sump lubrication to redesigned camshafts to the kind of lightweight forged pistons needed by some high-performance rides. In all, some 120 of the M159's components were upgraded compared to the M156.

Recent findings suggest that it's further worth pointing out that Mercedes refers to the engine as having 6.3 liters of displacement. You can chalk that up to marketing, however. To honor Mercedes' first post-war V8, the 6.3-liter M100, the company decided to also call the M156 a 6.3-liter mill — despite it displacing 6,208 cubic centimeters. That, obviously, should be rounded down to 6.2. Anyways, the naming strategy then carried over to the M159.

It has been revealed that as Chevy's high-performance halo car, it makes sense that the Corvette — especially in its ZR1 variants — has been the showcase for some of the brand's most powerful engines. So we're going to talk about two different versions of the Corvette's 6.2-liter V8: the LT5 from the 2019 ZR1, and the LS9 that came in the 2009 ZR1. First, it's the LS9.

Putting out a stout 638 horsepower, the LS9 is part of GM's long-running LS lineup, which is considered a totally different engine generation than the LT roster. One core practical difference is that the former featured port injection and the latter had direct injection, cylinder deactivation, and variable valve timing. Drilling down into the details indicates the LS and LT families are set apart by much more than that — there's practically zero parts interchangeability between the two.

The LS9 proved its performance credibility on the road with zero-to-60 sprints of 3.4 seconds and a top speed of 205 mph. When it debuted, it was Chevy's most powerful production motor.

When Chevrolet ended production of the front-engine Corvette, it sent the car out on top: The 2019 Chevrolet Corvette ZR1 debuted as the fastest, most powerful model to ever wear the Crossed Flags badge. Yes, both benchmarks have since been obliterated by the record-setting Corvette ZR1X, but the '19 ZR1 was no slouch. During testing at Car and Driver, the ZR1 covered the quarter mile in 10.7 seconds, reaching 135 mph along the way, and along the way it went from zero to 60 in 2.9 seconds.

Industry observers note that the engine backing those results was Chevy's supercharged 6.2-liter LT5 V8. Now, GM has a tendency to re-use its engine codes, so keep in mind that this is a totally different mill from the 5.7-liter LT5 V8 that Lotus developed for the 1990 ZR-1.

Sources indicate that oh, and the hand-built 2019 LT5 also set a record itself. The LT5's 755 hp and 715 lb-ft represented the most output ever offered in any production Chevy up to that point. Another milestone — the premiere of GM's first dual fuel-injection system — was a key contributor to the output. With that on board, the LT5 had both direct and port injection working for it.

In a recent development, before it was adapted to be fueled by ethanol and got a huge horsepower bump as a result, the "regular" Demon spent time as the most powerful muscle car in the world. Despite its street-legal status, the Demon was purpose-built for the dragstrip. There, it could make the most of its supercharged 6.2-liter V8 and enter the record books. The Demon tapped into 840 hp to cover the quarter mile in 9.65 seconds at 140 mph, making it the fastest production car in the quarter mile at the time.

The Demon was plenty different from its Hellcat predecessor. To be more specific, while it was technically the same engine, the Demon's V8 shared fewer than 40% of its components with the standard Hellcat. Notable enhancements here extended to a reinforced block with upgraded main caps and deck surfaces, along with a forged alloy crankshaft, forged pistons, and powder-forged connecting rods. Compared to the Demon's 840 hp, the standard Hellcat's 707 hp output seems almost pedestrian.

It has been revealed that dodge first debuted a supercharged 6.2-liter Hemi V8 for the 2015 Challenger SRT Hellcat, setting a template for the increasingly insane Dodge V8s that followed. The basic progression was from the Hellcat to the aforementioned Demon, and eventually to the Demon 170, with each set of changes significant enough to count as a different engine.

Consider the 2023 Dodge Challenger SRT Demon 170. The most powerful muscle car in the world when it released — according to Dodge – this street-legal stunner can spit out 1,250 hp and 945 lb-ft when drinking E85 ethanol fuel. On E10, it still offers up a hefty 900 horses. And although its supercharged 6.2-liter V8 shares its displacement with its predecessors, that's about all it shares. With the exception of the camshaft, just about every internal component on the Demon 170 was changed.

For one thing, to maximize its fluid intake, new fuel injectors capable of delivering more than 2.7 gallons of fuel per minute were used. On the air side of the fuel-air mixture, the 3.0-liter supercharger benefited from enhancements to its throttle body, pulley, intake valves, valve guides, bearings, connecting rods, and more. The outcome was a machine that could sprint to 60 in an EV-like 1.66 seconds on a race-prepped surface — just as fast as the Rimac Nevera R that set 24 new performance records in 2025.

#88351. 2026 Genesis GV80 Coupe Is An Appeal To Your Heart, Not Your Head

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Jalopnik ↗ Open Full Page

2026 Genesis GV80 Coupe Is An Appeal To Your Heart, Not Your Head

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1313 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Jalopnik

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Like just about everything Genesis makes, the GV80 Coupe is a fabulous-looking vehicle, perhaps the best-looking in its class with its distinctive front end, lovely silhouette and ducktail spoiler out back.
  • Sure, it runs on low-profile all-season rubber, has seat bolsters that hug you in corners, and is powered by a twin-turbocharged and electronically supercharged 3.5-liter V6.
  • Full Disclosure: Genesis was kind enough to lend me a 2026 GV80 Coupe with a full tank of fuel to do with as I pleased for a week.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Like just about everything Genesis makes, the GV80 Coupe is a fabulous-looking vehicle, perhaps the best-looking in its class with its distinctive front end, lovely silhouette and ducktail spoiler out back. And like most crossover coupes, the GV80 Coupe promises to lean more into the sporty side of things than its normal-backed brother. The thing is, it doesn't quite deliver on that.

Sure, it runs on low-profile all-season rubber, has seat bolsters that hug you in corners, and is powered by a twin-turbocharged and electronically supercharged 3.5-liter V6. It even has bright red seatbelts, but the GV80 Coupe is by no means a sports car. Hell, it's barely sporty and is certainly lacking a bit in the body control area when compared to stuff like the BMW X6 and Mercedes-Benz GLE Coupe. However, if you take the idea of sporty pretentions out of your head, you're in for a much better time, because the GV80 Coupe is a wonderful, delightfully comfortable cruiser with a well-thought-out interior, lots of top-notch luxury gizmos, and practicality that punches far above what you'd expect from a crossover coupe.

Full Disclosure: Genesis was kind enough to lend me a 2026 GV80 Coupe with a full tank of fuel to do with as I pleased for a week.

There are two engine options for the GV80 Coupe. A twin-turbocharged 3.5-liter V6 that pumps out 375 horsepower comes as standard, but those who aren't lilbabybois can step up to the more powerful (and certainly more interesting) twin-turbocharged 3.5-liter V6 that has a 48-volt system with an electric supercharger. This funky motor throws down 409 hp and 405 lb-ft of torque while also getting slightly better gas mileage than the standard motor. Don't worry, it's still not good fuel economy. The EPA rates it at 17 mpg city, 22 mpg highway and 19 mpg combined. It's a thirsty beast, but that's a small price to pay for all of this modest sportiness.

It has been revealed that granted, the GV80 E-SC, fitted with a Genesis-built 8-speed automatic that sends power to all four wheels, can get a move on in a straight line. It'll hit 60 mph from a standstill in 5.2 seconds, according to Car and Driver's testing, which is solid for a 5,132-pound crossover. The GV80 doesn't feel like it's in much of a rush to accelerate, though, and it also lags behind its competition. Without a doubt, it's a smooth powertrain, but it's not exactly sporty — not in the way the red seatbelts would imply.

The lack of sportiness becomes incredibly obvious when hustling the GV80 Coupe around a corner. It's almost as if those seatbelts are red not to denote sportiness, but to show how miffed the car is that I dare push it. The lack of athleticism is evident almost immediately, as the suspension and brakes have a tough time keeping up with the beefy curb weight. There's just too much body roll and not enough steering feel to make for any sort of fun-spirited driving no matter what drive mode I was in, including the E-Supercharged-exclusive Sport+ mode.

What I learned swiftly is that this car really shines as a cruiser. I've said in the past that crossover coupes are the personal luxury coupes of the modern age, and that's true again with the GV80 Coupe. This thing is wonderfully comfortable to eat highway miles in or blast around town as the Ergo Motion driver's seat works on that knot in my back and HMG's wonderful suite of driver-assistance aids keep me in my lane and out of the rear bumper of the car in front of me. The engine, while interesting in its operation, doesn't provide the most inspiring noise, so it's not the end of the world when it shuts up as I drive in quiet, calm luxury through the streets of Fresh York.

It has been revealed that beyond those lovely quilted leather seats, the interior of the GV80 Coupe is a fantastic place to be that also goes toward its cruising pretensions. Sure, there's some carbon-fiber-look trim, but it doesn't exactly scream sportiness. Neither does the wood, metal, glass, and swaths of suede. Do ya know what that does scream? Nice. Pleasant. Chill. Good.

Another nice, pleasant, chill, and good element of the GV80's interior is its 27-inch OLED touchscreen that serves as both a digital gauge cluster and center infotainment display. Inputs can be made with either fingers or an iDrive-style control knob. I'll admit, the system feels a bit clunky to use the first day or so, a step behind BMW and Mercedes-Benz's new systems, but after a bit of learning where everything else is, it becomes second nature. Using wireless Apple CarPlay and Android Auto fixes that problem quickly, too. Adding to the simplicity is the secondary touchscreen below it that has all of the car's climate controls housed within it, and between the two screens is a row of buttons that can pull up core vehicle controls. It's certainly welcome for the Luddites among us.

It has been revealed that aside from the sloping roofline, not too much else was changed on the inside or outside for the Coupe, which isn't a bad thing as the GV80 is a lovely-looking vehicle from the get-go. The GV80 Coupe carries the same 116.3-inch wheelbase as the regular GV80, but overall length increases by an inch to 195.5 inches, and the rakish roofline drops overall height by 0.2 inches. Rear seat occupants probably aren't going to miss the 0.8 inches of headroom they've given up, and if they are ones to complain, ditch them. You don't need that sort of negativity in your life, anyway. You're going to need to trim the fat regardless, because there's no third row in the Coupe.

Industry observers note that the GV80 Coupe is no exception when it comes to crossover coupes being a bit silly. No truly practical person would buy one over the normal crossover they're based on simply because they're an exercise in style over substance. They're innately compromised products, and on top of that, they almost always cost more.

A base-base GV80 2.5T RWD starts at $59,195 including destination, but that's not really a fair comparison, so let's look at the GV80 3.5T Advanced AWD — that's the trim level where the Coupe starts from. The regular GV80 in that spec starts at $77,445, while a comparable GV80 Coupe is going to be $83,345. That means you, dear buyer, need to fork over an extra $5,900 for the pleasure of having fewer seats and worse visibility out the rear. I, however, would contend that that is a small price to pay for such a pretty car. Argue with a wall.

The GV80 I drove was no base-spec, though, as it had the E-Supercharger, boosting its starting price to $89,145. The vehicle's lone option, $650 worth of Bering Blue Paint, brought the final price to $89,795. It's a small price to pay for something that looks this good — it's nearly a concept car for the road, if you ask me. If you think of the GV80 Coupe as a piece of art rather than a car, then it's a hell of a deal, and it's even fairly in line with alternatives from Germany like the Mercedes-Benz GLE450 Coupe ($82,650), Audi Q8 Premium ($78,295), BMW X6 40i xDrive ($78,750) and Porsche Cayenne Coupe ($97,450). It's worth the premium over the latter four based on looks alone.

In a recent development, of course, if you look at it compared to the normal GV80, things fall apart, but this is a car meant to speak to your heart, not your head. Just take a second to look at the mess your head's gotten you into throughout your life. Perhaps it's time to let your heart make some decisions.

Is AI A Public Or A Private Asset?

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1114 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cleantechnica

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that isabelle Ferreras is a professor and research director at the University of Louvain, an Accelerator fellow at the Institute for Ethics in AI at the University of Oxford, and a senior research associate at the Center for Labor and a Just Economy at Harvard University.
  • She told The Guardian this week that she has grave concerns about the way AI and the corporations promoting it are managing this brave new technology.
  • Last month, a person responsible for overseeing safety reports at OpenAI left the company, claiming its culture was “broken.” He added that the entire AI industry was careless when it comes to developing AI technology.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that isabelle Ferreras is a professor and research director at the University of Louvain, an Accelerator fellow at the Institute for Ethics in AI at the University of Oxford, and a senior research associate at the Center for Labor and a Just Economy at Harvard University. It safe to say she knows a thing or two about computer technology and AI.

She told The Guardian this week that she has grave concerns about the way AI and the corporations promoting it are managing this brave new technology. Her concerns are spurred by the number of high profile computer engineers who have quit recently over fears that AI development is out of control.

Last month, a person responsible for overseeing safety reports at OpenAI left the company, claiming its culture was “broken.” He added that the entire AI industry was careless when it comes to developing AI technology. The month before that, a researcher at Anthropic — which went public yesterday at a valuation $1.8 trillion dollars — warned that AI “could kill us all by the end of the decade.”.

Recent findings suggest that “When the only way for a conscientious engineer to raise the alarm is to leave,” Ferreras mentioned. “it is a clear sign that corporate governance in the industry is broken. Each departure takes with it the very knowledge needed to steer these systems safely. We cannot regulate AI safely from the outside if the companies building it remain autocracies on the inside.”.

Ferreras warned that governments think of AI either as a “consumer product to be tested for defects or as a geopolitical race to be won by relaxing rules on business. Corporate lobbyists encourage this view as a trade-off between safety and innovation by arguing that legislation imposes too many burdens.

“This is a dangerous path. AI is not merely a software product. It is a technology of government. Yet inside frontier labs such as OpenAI, Anthropic, Microsoft, and Google, a handful of executives and capital investors decide which values are coded into models that shape millions of lives,” she mentioned.

According to recent reports, interestingly, Michael Connolly, the award winning author of the Bosch and Lincoln Lawyer novels, published a book last year in which the family of a young woman, who was murdered by her boyfriend after he interacted with an AI agent, sues the organization behind the AI agent. The essence of the lawsuit is that AI only does what it is programmed to do, and since the lead programmer of this particular AI agent was a misogynist in real life, it reflected his values when it interacted with humans. The book is called The Proving Ground and it is a fascinating read.

Industry observers note that while Ferreras applauds those who warn of the malignancies built into AI, she pointed out that humans have short attention spans. “Time and again, a safety researcher or engineer walks out of the door with a public warning that commercial pressures are overriding safety guardrails. As a society, we applaud the courage of these individuals and debate their warnings for a news cycle — and then we move on. But we miss the deeper institutional failure those resignations reveal. As the great political scientist Albert Hirschman made clear, exit is not voice.”.

It has been revealed that in a democratic society, the exercise of governing power requires the consent of the governed, Ferreras told The Guardian. “Yet corporate law still treats firms as the property of shareholders, and the labor investors, who put their intellect, health and lives into the firm, as subordinates. To align AI with the public interest, we need a dual strategy: alongside solid public regulations on AI ‘from the outside,’ we need to enter the corporate black box and force corporate governance into alignment with democratic principles.”.

In a recent development, an analogy can be made to the Federal Communications Commission, which licenses broadcasters and promotes the free flow of information to the public. The digital world thinks such controls are archaic, but the lack of them is a clear and present danger to a civil society.

Sources indicate that ferreras suggested that “governments must outlaw non-disclosure and non-disparagement clauses that silence staff on safety risks, and enact robust whistle blower protection. Tech workers also need a collective standing over corporate strategy, independent channels to report safety breaches, and formal representation inside frontier labs before models are deployed.”.

According to recent reports, in addition, she argued that “legislators must establish a binding right to co-decision over workplace AI. No algorithmic system that monitors, evaluates or disciplines workers should be deployed without prior negotiation. At national and EU level, we need to consider collective bargaining on AI deployment and veto rights for works councils or trade unions, backed by independent technical experts and a strict ban on automated firing.”.

According to recent reports, lastly, she supported the democratization of boardrooms and rewarding firms that refuse to concentrate power at the top. “Legislators should mandate worker-elected directors on boards, moving towards dual-majority governance in which strategic decisions require the consent not only of capital but of labor.” Some, like Elon Musk and Mark Zuckerberg, would characterize her suggestions as liberal claptrap, and they would be correct. Ferreras would happily unravel the “tech bro” manosphere in order to promote a more open and just society.

She pointed to the research by Daron Acemoglu and Simon Johnson, the 2024 Nobel laureates in economics, which demonstrates that technological revolutions do not automatically produce shared prosperity. Instead, institutions decide who benefits and who pays.

Sources indicate that “Extending democracy into the firm is not an old battle over power for its own sake, but a practical necessity for more ethical judgment. Aligning AI with the good of workers and society requires more wisdom than closed executive rooms can offer. It needs what the Yale political theorist Hélène Landemore calls ‘democratic reason’ — the collective intelligence of diverse, deliberating voices, brought to bear on corporate decision-making,” Ferreras wrote.

“Left to self-regulation and the occasional whistleblower, AI governance will entrench an unaccountable algorithmic oligarchy. Accountability and alignment begins with giving those who build these systems and those whose work they govern an enforceable voice, from the code floor to the boardroom.”.

Ferreras’ point of view is decidedly liberal, and yet her arguments are clear and concise. How can we give so much power to digital agents and not take reasonable steps to ensure the needs of society as a whole are respected? The tech industry enjoys almost unfettered freedom of action today. It may be time to consider whether that is a good long term strategy.
